name: Machine Tools Family (Mills, Drills, Presses, Grinders)
region: Global (China, Islamic world, Europe, North America, Japan)
summary: The lineage of rotary and reciprocating tools — mills, drills, boring machines, presses, and grinders — descended from lathe principles and metallurgical advances, enabling the production of interchangeable parts.

claims.statement: Bow drills appear in archaeological records from Egypt and Mesopotamia by 1200 BCE, and independently in Mesoamerica, establishing rotary tool principles before the formalisation of the lathe
Islamic-era engineers developed water-powered trip hammers, cam-driven mills, and crankshaft mechanisms that formed the mechanical vocabulary later adopted by European industrialisation

Maudslay's screw-cutting lathe (1800) and Wilkinson's boring machine (1774) created the precision feedback loop: better machine tools produce better machine tools, enabling the Industrial Revolution's interchangeable-parts paradigm

evidence.source: Stocks (2003) Experiments in Egyptian Archaeology: Stoneworking Technology in Ancient Egypt, Routledge
Al-Hassan & Hill (1986) Islamic Technology: An Illustrated History, Cambridge UP / UNESCO
Rolt (1965) Tools for the Job: A Short History of Machine Tools, Batsford; rev. ed. MIT Press 1986
Rosenberg (1963) Technological Change in the Machine Tool Industry, 1840–1910, Journal of Economic History 23(4)

notes: Resolves 3 inbound links (lathe, precision_engineering, damascus_steel). The self-reinforcing feedback loop — better tools make better tools — is the defining feature. Islamic-era contributions are critical and often under-documented in Western narratives.
